## Preface — the second draft {.unnumbered}

The original curriculum (`better_graphs.qmd`, M0–M7) taught the craft: hold object handles,
choose the chart before you code, polish away the "default matplotlib" tell. This document is
its second draft, written green-field by a different author with the same convictions and a
sharper claim:

> **A figure is a small publication.** It has a headline, a standfirst (the *dek*), a body,
> and a source line. It is edited for a specific reader with a specific attention budget.
> Everything on it is either evidence or is cut.

Three questions, asked in order, decide every figure — the full argument lives in
[`STYLE_AND_SUBSTANCE.md`](../STYLE_AND_SUBSTANCE.md):

1. **What am I saying?** One sentence, before any code. `VISUALIZATION_GUIDE.md` turns it
   into a chart choice.
2. **Who is reading?** The **register** — `glance` (3 seconds, across a room), `read`
   (30 seconds, arm's length), `study` (minutes, leaning in).
3. **How hard should I try?** The **altitude** — A0 themed default, A1 composed chart,
   A2 bespoke drawing with raw Artists. Effort is a budget; most figures live at A1.

::: {.callout-note}
This chapter of the project was designed and written by **Claude Fable 5** (Anthropic), asked
to reimagine the repo's house style from scratch — research, palette mathematics, module,
prose, and figures — under the owner's direction. The system it built is named after its
author: *fable*. The original M0–M7 curriculum by Claude Opus 4.8 remains the craft course;
nothing here replaces it, everything here argues with it a little.
:::

```{python}
#| label: setup
# The page anatomy uses inch-true margins, so the notebook renderer must not
# tight-crop them away.
%config InlineBackend.print_figure_kwargs = {'bbox_inches': None}

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import fable
from ndata import load, select, group, pivot, MONTHS

fable.theme("read")   # question 2 gets answered before the first mark is drawn
```

# The thesis — decluttered is only half the work

**Principle.** Tufte's data-ink razor is a *precondition*, not the payoff. In the controlled
experiments of Ajani, Xiong, Knaflic & Franconeri, decluttered charts scored no better than
cluttered ones on ten-second recall. The winners were ***focused*** charts: decluttered,
**plus** one accented series, **plus** a plain-language annotation stating the conclusion.
Cleaning tells the reader you're serious; the accent and the sentence tell them what you found.

Three renderings of the same twelve numbers — yearly passengers on international airlines.

## Cluttered — the raw default

```{python}
#| label: thesis-cluttered
#| fig-cap: "The raw default: boxed in, primary blue, a title that renames the y-axis, no finding in sight."
flights = load("flights")
year, passengers_per_year = group(flights["year"], flights["passengers"].astype(float), np.nansum)

# style.use, not style.context: generic font families resolve at DRAW time, which
# happens after a context manager exits — a context here would render this
# "default" figure in the fable fonts. (fable.theme() restores the system later.)
plt.style.use("default")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(year, passengers_per_year, marker="o")
ax.set_title("passengers")
ax.set_xlabel("year")
ax.set_ylabel("passengers")
ax.grid(True)
```

## Decluttered — necessary, not sufficient

```{python}
#| label: thesis-decluttered
#| fig-cap: "Decluttered: spines trimmed, grid faded, junk gone — and still no finding. The reader does all the work."
plt.style.use("default")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(year, passengers_per_year, color="#666666", lw=2)
for side in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#dddddd", lw=0.7)
ax.set_title("Airline passengers per year", loc="left")
```

## Focused — the fable page

```{python}
#| label: thesis-focused
#| fig-cap: "Focused: the same numbers as a publication — kicker, a title with a verb, units in the dek, an annotation that interprets, a source line."
fable.theme("read")
fig, ax = fable.page(
    kicker="Air travel · 1949–1960",
    title="The jet age took off before the jets did",
    dek="Passengers on international airlines, millions per year. The Boeing 707's\n"
        "1958 debut only steepened a climb already under way.",
    source="Source: Box & Jenkins airline series, via seaborn-data",
    note="better graphs · fable",
)
ax.plot(year, passengers_per_year / 1e3, color=fable.ACCENT, zorder=3)
fable.gradient_fill(ax, year, passengers_per_year / 1e3, alpha_top=0.10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 6)
ax.margins(x=0.02)
fable.finish(ax)
fable.units(ax, "y", "count")
passengers_1958_k = passengers_per_year[year == 1958][0] / 1e3
fable.mark(ax, 1958, passengers_1958_k, "707 enters service",
           dx=-64, dy=26, color=fable.INK)
```

The anatomy, top to bottom: the violet **tab** (the brand device — it never moves), a tracked
**kicker** naming topic and period, a **title** that states the finding in League Spartan, a
**dek** in Junction carrying what/units/method, the plot with y-labels sitting *on* their
gridlines and a bottom rule that ends where the data ends, and a **source line** — because a
figure that leaves the room must carry its provenance.

## The first draft, for the record

fable is a second draft, so the honest before/after is against the *original house style*,
not just against raw matplotlib. Here is the same series drawn exactly as `main`'s
`house_style` draws it (this is the README's `line-after.png`):

```{python}
#| label: thesis-house-style
#| fig-cap: "The first draft — main's house style. Clean, accented, takeaway-titled… and still: no units, no source, no interpretation. A tidied chart, not yet a publication."
import house_style

house_style.apply_theme("executive")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.5))
ax.plot(year, passengers_per_year, color=house_style.ACCENT, lw=2.6)
house_style.polish(ax, grid="y")
house_style.thousands(ax, "y")
ax.margins(x=0.10)
ax.annotate(f"{passengers_per_year[-1]:,.0f}", (year[-1], passengers_per_year[-1]),
            xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center",
            color=house_style.ACCENT, fontsize=11, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Air travel ~doubled across the 1950s", loc="left", pad=10)
```

Both drafts share the convictions — OO API, takeaway title, accent over grey, trimmed
spines. What the second draft adds is exactly the publication layer: the **units** ("5,714"
of *what*?), the **source line**, the **kicker** giving context, the **dek** doing the work a
legend and a y-label used to fail at, and one **interpretive annotation**. Same taste,
higher resolution.

::: {.callout-important}
## Extract — the thesis rules
1. **Decluttering is a precondition; the accent + interpretive annotation are the payoff.**
   A polished figure with no stated finding is unfinished.
2. **The anatomy is the API:** `fable.page(kicker=, title=, dek=, source=)` — units in the
   dek, never a rotated y-label; a title with a verb, never centred.
3. `fable.save()` exports with the margins intact — never `bbox_inches="tight"` on a page.
:::

# The register — one dataset, three readers

**Principle.** A slide seen for three seconds, a report read at arm's length, and an appendix
studied by an expert are three different *contracts*. Same data, three figures —
`fable.theme()` makes the contract explicit before the first mark is drawn.

The finding, one sentence: **Gentoo penguins run about a kilogram heavier than Adélie and
chinstrap.**

## `glance` — three seconds, across a room

```{python}
#| label: register-glance
#| fig-cap: "The glance register: one message, one accent, direct labels, aggressive rounding. Nothing to decode."
fable.theme("glance")
penguins = load("penguins")
species_order = np.array(["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"])
species_labels = ["Adélie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]      # display names, one spelling everywhere
mass_by_species = [penguins["body_mass_g"][penguins["species"] == s] / 1000
                   for s in species_order]

fig, ax = fable.page(
    size=(9.0, 4.6),
    kicker="Palmer penguins",
    title="Gentoo run a kilogram heavier",
    dek="Body mass by species, kg. Each dot is one bird.",
    source="Source: Palmer Station LTER, via seaborn-data",
    margin_left=1.0,      # room for the species labels
)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
for row, (species, masses) in enumerate(zip(species_order, mass_by_species)):
    is_gentoo = species == "Gentoo"
    color = fable.ACCENT if is_gentoo else fable.CONTEXT
    jitter = rng.normal(0, 0.06, masses.size)
    ax.scatter(masses, row + jitter, s=26, color=color, alpha=0.45, lw=0)
    ax.scatter([masses.mean()], [row], s=230, color=color, zorder=5,
               edgecolor=fable.PAPER, lw=1.4)
    ax.annotate(f"{masses.mean():.1f} kg", (masses.mean(), row),
                xytext=(0, 16), textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                family=fable.DISPLAY_STACK, weight=600,
                size=15 if is_gentoo else 12,
                color=color if is_gentoo else fable.MUTED)
ax.set_yticks(range(3))
ax.set_yticklabels(species_labels, family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=12)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 2.75)
fable.finish(ax, grid=None)
ax.set_xticks([3, 4, 5, 6])
fable.units(ax, "x", "count")
```

## `read` — thirty seconds, arm's length

```{python}
#| label: register-read
#| fig-cap: "The read register: the relationship behind the ranking, series colour-keyed into the dek — the legend, dissolved."
fable.theme("read")
flipper_mm = penguins["flipper_length_mm"]
body_mass_kg = penguins["body_mass_g"] / 1000
species = penguins["species"]

fig, ax = fable.page(
    kicker="Palmer penguins · 344 birds",
    title="Bigger flippers, heavier birds — and Gentoo own the top-right",
    dek="Body mass in kg against flipper length: <Gentoo> sit a kilogram\n"
        "above <Adélie> and <Chinstrap> at every flipper size.",
    dek_highlights=[{"color": fable.ACCENT, "weight": 700},
                    {"color": fable.EMERALD, "weight": 700},
                    {"color": fable.OCHRE, "weight": 700}],
    source="Source: Palmer Station LTER, via seaborn-data",
)
species_colors = {"Gentoo": fable.ACCENT, "Adelie": fable.EMERALD, "Chinstrap": fable.OCHRE}
for name, color in species_colors.items():
    of_species = species == name
    ax.scatter(flipper_mm[of_species], body_mass_kg[of_species],
               s=26, color=color, alpha=0.55, lw=0)
fable.finish(ax)
fable.units(ax, "y", "count")
# glyph fallback (the arrow) only engages when the font stack is explicit
ax.set_xlabel("flipper length (mm) →", loc="right", family=fable.BODY_STACK)
```

## `study` — minutes, leaning in

```{python}
#| label: register-study
#| fig-cap: "The study register: the full distributions, exact means, and n on the figure. Density is welcome; vagueness is not."
fable.theme("study")
fig, panels = fable.page(
    size=(9.6, 4.4), mosaic="ACG",
    kicker="Palmer penguins · body mass",
    title="The Gentoo shift is the whole distribution, not a tail",
    dek="Body mass distributions by species, kg. Bin width 250 g; dashed rule at each mean.",
    source="Source: Palmer Station LTER, via seaborn-data · n = 342 after dropping 2 incomplete records",
    wspace=0.12, gap_below_dek=0.30,
)
bins = np.arange(2.5, 6.75, 0.25)
panel_names = {"Adelie": "A", "Chinstrap": "C", "Gentoo": "G"}
for name, key in panel_names.items():
    panel = panels[key]
    masses = penguins["body_mass_g"][penguins["species"] == name] / 1000
    is_gentoo = name == "Gentoo"
    panel.hist(masses, bins=bins, color=fable.ACCENT if is_gentoo else fable.CONTEXT,
               edgecolor=fable.PAPER, lw=0.6)
    panel.axvline(masses.mean(), ls=(0, (4, 3)), lw=1.1, color=fable.INK)
    panel.annotate(f"mean {masses.mean():.2f} kg\nn = {masses.size}",
                   xy=(0.97, 0.93), xycoords="axes fraction", ha="right", va="top",
                   family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=8.5, color=fable.MUTED)
    fable.panel_title(panel, "Adélie" if name == "Adelie" else name)
    panel.sharey(panels["A"])
    fable.finish(panel, grid="y", nbins=4)
for key in ("C", "G"):
    panels[key].tick_params(labelleft=False)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Extract — the register rules
1. **State the register before plotting**, right after the chart choice: *"`read`, because
   this goes in the report body."* `fable.theme(register)` is the first plotting line.
2. **One figure, one register.** Never reuse a slide figure in an appendix — re-render.
3. The register caps everything: series count, tick budget, annotation budget, novelty.
   The table lives in `STYLE_AND_SUBSTANCE.md`.
:::

# Colour — computed, not eyeballed

**Principle.** A palette is a claim — *"these colours are distinguishable, by everyone, on
this background"* — and the claim is checkable by simulation. Taste chooses the candidates;
arithmetic gets a veto.

## The receipts

The palette that leads this system (violet · emerald · ochre · wine · navy · rust) was chosen
by exactly that loop: hand-picked hue families, then `check_palette.py` simulating three kinds
of dichromacy (Machado 2009) and measuring worst-pair ΔE, lightness band, chroma floor, and
contrast against the paper. Run it — on the *old* house palette and on fable's:

```{python}
#| label: color-receipts
from check_palette import check

minerva_palette = ["#6400FF", "#1AA7A0", "#E8833A", "#C44E9C", "#5A8F3C", "#2D7DD2"]
fable_palette = fable.SERIES

for name, palette in [("minerva (main)", minerva_palette), ("fable", fable_palette)]:
    report = check(palette, bg=fable.PAPER)
    worst = {condition: result["min_delta_e"]
             for condition, result in report["separation"].items()}
    print(f"{name:15s} ok={report['ok']!s:5s} worst-pair deltaE by condition: {worst}")
```

The old palette's orange/green pair collapses to ΔE ≈ 7 under protanopia — indistinguishable
for roughly one in twelve male readers, and invisible to anyone squinting at swatches. That is
why **palette changes go through the validator**, and why the fable palette clears every
condition with more than twice the ΔE ≥ 12 target.

## Sequential — one hue, honestly spaced

```{python}
#| label: color-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "The flights matrix on the house sequential ramp — Lab-arc-length equalised so equal steps read as equal change. The peak is labelled because the colorbar alone can't say '622'."
fable.theme("read")
years = np.unique(flights["year"])
month_names, _, passenger_matrix = pivot(
    flights["month"], flights["year"], flights["passengers"], rows=MONTHS, cols=years)

fig, ax = fable.page(
    size=(8.6, 5.2),
    kicker="Air travel · monthly, 1949–1960",
    title="Every summer peaks higher than the last",
    dek="Passengers per month. The July 1960 peak is nearly six times January 1949.",
    source="Source: Box & Jenkins airline series, via seaborn-data",
    margin_right=0.9,
)
heat = ax.pcolormesh(years, np.arange(12), passenger_matrix,
                     cmap=fable.SEQUENTIAL, rasterized=True)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(12), [m[:3] for m in MONTHS], family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=8.5)
ax.set_xticks(years[1::2])                       # 1950 … 1960: the peak column gets its year
ax.grid(False)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
for spine in ax.spines.values():   # a hairline frame so the palest cells read as data
    spine.set_visible(True)
    spine.set_edgecolor(fable.HAIRLINE)
    spine.set_linewidth(0.8)
colorbar = fig.colorbar(heat, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.03)
colorbar.set_ticks([200, 400, 600], labels=["200", "400", "600k"])   # unit on the top tick
colorbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8.5, length=0)
colorbar.outline.set_visible(False)
peak_month, peak_year = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(passenger_matrix), passenger_matrix.shape)
peak_value = passenger_matrix[peak_month, peak_year]
ax.annotate(f"{peak_value:,.0f}k", xy=(years[peak_year], peak_month),
            ha="center", va="center", family=fable.BODY_STACK, weight=700,
            size=9, color=fable.PAPER)
```

## Diverging — two hues around a meaningful zero

```{python}
#| label: color-diverging
#| fig-cap: "Signed change wants a diverging encoding centred at zero: violet for gains, rust for losses, printed values on every bar."
gapminder = load("gapminder")
africa = select(gapminder, gapminder["continent"] == "Africa")
countries_1987 = select(africa, africa["year"] == 1987)
countries_2007 = select(africa, africa["year"] == 2007)
assert (countries_1987["country"] == countries_2007["country"]).all()
life_exp_change = countries_2007["lifeExp"] - countries_1987["lifeExp"]

biggest_moves = np.argsort(life_exp_change)
show = np.concatenate([biggest_moves[:6], biggest_moves[-6:]])
show = show[np.argsort(life_exp_change[show])]
change_shown = life_exp_change[show]
names_shown = countries_1987["country"][show]

fable.theme("read")
fig, ax = fable.page(
    size=(7.6, 5.4),
    kicker="Gapminder · Africa, 1987–2007",
    title="Twenty years that moved in both directions",
    dek="Change in life expectancy at birth, years. The AIDS epidemic reversed decades\n"
        "of gains in southern Africa while West Africa kept climbing.",
    source="Source: Gapminder via Rdatasets · six biggest declines and six biggest gains shown",
    margin_left=1.05,     # room for the country labels
    margin_bottom=0.55,   # no x axis, so don't reserve tick space — keeps the footer anchored
)
bar_colors = [fable.BAD if change < 0 else fable.ACCENT for change in change_shown]
rows = np.arange(len(show))
ax.barh(rows, change_shown, height=0.62, color=bar_colors)
ax.vlines(0, -0.5, len(show) - 0.5, color=fable.INK, lw=1.1)   # zero rule spans the bars, no more
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(show) - 0.3)
for row, change in zip(rows, change_shown):
    inside = f"{change:+.1f}".replace("-", "−")   # a true minus, not a hyphen
    ax.annotate(inside, (change, row), xytext=(5 if change > 0 else -5, 0),
                textcoords="offset points", va="center",
                ha="left" if change > 0 else "right",
                family=fable.BODY_STACK, weight=700, size=8.5,
                color=bar_colors[row])
ax.set_yticks(rows, names_shown, family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=9)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
ax.grid(False)
for side in ("bottom",):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.margins(x=0.14)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Extract — the colour rules
1. **Palettes are computed, not eyeballed** — `check_palette.py` before any palette ships;
   simulate the rendered figure when lines are thin.
2. **Fixed assignment, never cycled**: violet is always series 1; a 7th series is a design
   failure. `GOOD`/`BAD` are reserved status colours.
3. Sequential = one hue, perceptually spaced (`fable.SEQUENTIAL`, or viridis). Diverging =
   two hues meeting at a light neutral, centred on the meaningful zero (`diverging_norm`).
   Signed data on a sequential ramp is a lie of omission.
:::

# The altitude — how hard to try

**Principle.** Craft is a budget. A0 (themed default) is for your own eyes; A1 (composed) is
the default for anything shared; A2 (bespoke Artists) must pass a four-gate test: the message
survives a standard form → the standard form buries it *or* the form carries meaning → the
audience × lifetime pays for the craft → it stays honest. Most figures should fail gate 3.
The same twelve years of seasonality, at all three altitudes:

## A0 — the themed default (exploration only)

```{python}
#| label: altitude-a0
#| fig-cap: "A0: twelve month-lines under the theme. Fine for a first look at your own screen; spaghetti for anyone else."
fable.theme("read")
fig, ax = fable.page(title="A0 — the exploratory look", tab=False)
for month_index, month in enumerate(MONTHS):
    ax.plot(years, passenger_matrix[month_index], lw=1.2)
fable.finish(ax)
```

## A1 — the composed chart (the cycle plot)

```{python}
#| label: altitude-a1
#| fig-cap: "A1: a cycle plot — one small panel per month, the right 'standard' chart almost nobody reaches for. Structure AND trend, no spaghetti."
fable.theme("study")
fig, panels = fable.page(
    size=(9.8, 4.6), mosaic="ABCDEFGHIJKL",
    kicker="Air travel · monthly, 1949–1960",
    title="Summer grows fastest — the season is the story",
    dek="Passengers per month, thousands; each panel runs 1949 to 1960, and the rule marks the month's mean.\n"
        "July and August didn't just start higher — they grew faster than any other month.",
    source="Source: Box & Jenkins airline series, via seaborn-data",
    wspace=0.14, gap_below_dek=0.26,
)
summer = {"July", "August"}
for month_index, (month, key) in enumerate(zip(MONTHS, "ABCDEFGHIJKL")):
    panel = panels[key]
    is_summer = month in summer
    monthly = passenger_matrix[month_index]
    panel.plot(years, monthly, lw=1.9 if is_summer else 1.2,
               color=fable.ACCENT if is_summer else fable.CONTEXT)
    panel.axhline(np.nanmean(monthly), lw=0.8, color=fable.MUTED, alpha=0.6)
    panel.set_title(month[:3], family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=8.5, pad=4,
                    color=fable.ACCENT if is_summer else fable.MUTED,
                    weight=700 if is_summer else 500)
    panel.sharey(panels["A"])
    panel.set_xticks([])
    panel.set_yticks([0, 200, 400, 600])
    panel.grid(axis="y", color=fable.HAIRLINE, lw=0.5)   # anchors the shared y labels
    panel.set_axisbelow(True)
    for spine in panel.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(False)
    panel.tick_params(length=0, labelleft=key == "A", labelsize=8)
panels["A"].set_ylim(0, 700)
```

## A2 — the bespoke form (the seasonal spiral)

Gate check, aloud: the finding survives a standard form (the cycle plot above) ✓; a linear
axis *buries the cycle* — December and January are neighbours the line chart tears apart, and
the form itself carries the meaning ✓; this is a poster/README hero, seen by many ✓; radius
starts at zero and the values stay readable ✓. Passed — so we throw the axes away and draw.

```{python}
#| label: altitude-a2
#| fig-cap: "A2: twelve years wound into a spiral — time as a helix, the season as an angle. The form IS the message; the how-to-read key is part of the figure."
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection

fable.theme("glance")
fig, ax = fable.page(
    size=(8.6, 8.2),
    kicker="Air travel · monthly, 1949–1960",
    title="Twelve years of summers, wound tight",
    dek="Each turn is one year, January at the top; distance from centre and colour\n"
        "both encode passengers per month.",
    source="Source: Box & Jenkins airline series, via seaborn-data",
    tab=True,
)
passengers_flat = passenger_matrix.T.reshape(-1)          # year-major: Jan 1949 … Dec 1960
month_in_series = np.arange(passengers_flat.size)
angle = -2 * np.pi * (month_in_series % 12) / 12 + np.pi / 2   # Jan at 12 o'clock, clockwise
radius = passengers_flat
x = radius * np.cos(angle)
y = radius * np.sin(angle)

points = np.column_stack([x, y]).reshape(-1, 1, 2)
segments = np.concatenate([points[:-1], points[1:]], axis=1)
spiral = LineCollection(segments, cmap=fable.SEQUENTIAL, capstyle="round",
                        array=passengers_flat[:-1], linewidths=2.4)
ax.add_collection(spiral)

# hand-drawn polar furniture: rings at 200/400/600k, spokes at each month
import matplotlib.patheffects as pe

ring_theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 240)
for ring in (200, 400, 600):
    ax.plot(ring * np.cos(ring_theta), ring * np.sin(ring_theta),
            lw=0.7, color=fable.HAIRLINE, zorder=0)
    ax.annotate(f"{ring}k", (0, ring), xytext=(0, 3), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=8, color=fable.FAINT,
                path_effects=[pe.withStroke(linewidth=2.6, foreground=fable.PAPER)])
for month_index, month in enumerate(MONTHS):
    spoke = -2 * np.pi * month_index / 12 + np.pi / 2
    ax.annotate(month[:3], (720 * np.cos(spoke), 720 * np.sin(spoke)),
                ha="center", va="center", family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=9,
                color=fable.MUTED)
peak = int(np.argmax(passengers_flat))          # July 1960, the all-time high
fable.mark(ax, x[peak], y[peak], f"Jul 1960 · {passengers_flat[peak]:,.0f}k",
           dx=-96, dy=-34, color=fable.INK)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(-800, 800)
ax.set_ylim(-800, 800)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

The honest verdict: for a `study` reader the **cycle plot wins** — it supports precise
comparison, the spiral doesn't. The spiral earns its place only where a poster needs to *stop
traffic* and the printed labels pay the debt. That's the altitude ladder working as intended:
the test told us **when**, the Artists told us **how**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Extract — the altitude rules
1. **A1 is the default for anything shared.** A0 never leaves your screen.
2. **A2 requires the four-gate test, spoken aloud** — and gate 4 (honesty: zero-based radii,
   printed values, a how-to-read key) is non-negotiable.
3. Bespoke work is still made of the same Artists — `LineCollection`, hand-drawn rings,
   `annotate` — under the same theme. Bespoke means *composed by hand*, not *lawless*.
:::

# Bespoke craft — drawing an instrument, not a chart

**Principle.** Some data has a geometry of its own. An antenna pattern is not a time series —
it is a *shape in space*, and the reader's question ("where does the energy go?") is angular.
Default polar axes answer it with clutter; forty lines of Artists answer it like a datasheet
figure should. This is the A2 chapter: every ring, spoke and label placed on purpose.

```{python}
#| label: bespoke-antenna
#| fig-cap: "An 8-element array pattern drawn as an instrument: dB rings as depth, the main lobe accented, beamwidth measured on the figure, sidelobes labelled. No default polar furniture survives."
antenna = load("rf_antenna_pattern")
angle_deg = antenna["angle_deg"]
gain_db = antenna["gain_db"]

# measure first, so the title can state what the figure proves
main_lobe = np.abs(angle_deg) <= 14.4                    # first nulls of the 8-element array
above_half_power = (gain_db >= -3) & main_lobe
half_power_angles = angle_deg[above_half_power]
beamwidth = half_power_angles[-1] - half_power_angles[0]
sidelobe_region = (angle_deg > 14.4) & (angle_deg < 30)
sidelobe_index = np.flatnonzero(sidelobe_region)[np.argmax(gain_db[sidelobe_region])]
sidelobe_db = gain_db[sidelobe_index]

fable.theme("read")
fig, ax = fable.page(
    size=(9.2, 6.4),
    kicker="8-element uniform linear array · half-wavelength spacing",
    title=f"A {beamwidth:.1f}° beam, sidelobes {abs(sidelobe_db):.1f} dB down",
    dek="Normalised gain vs. angle from broadside; radial depth in dB, floor at −40 dB.",
    source="Source: synthesized ULA pattern (data/build_datasets.py)",
)

FLOOR_DB = -40.0
def db_to_radius(db):
    return (np.asarray(db) - FLOOR_DB) / -FLOOR_DB      # −40 dB → 0, 0 dB → 1

theta = np.deg2rad(angle_deg)                            # 0° = broadside, straight up
pattern_x = db_to_radius(gain_db) * np.sin(theta)
pattern_y = db_to_radius(gain_db) * np.cos(theta)

# furniture first: dB rings and angle spokes, drawn by hand so they stop mattering
import matplotlib.patheffects as pe

half_circle = np.linspace(-np.pi / 2, np.pi / 2, 181)
for ring_db in (0, -10, -20, -30):
    ring_r = db_to_radius(ring_db)
    ax.plot(ring_r * np.sin(half_circle), ring_r * np.cos(half_circle),
            lw=0.7, color=fable.HAIRLINE, zorder=0)
    ax.annotate(f"{ring_db:g}".replace("-", "−") + (" dB" if ring_db == 0 else ""),
                (-0.025, ring_r + 0.008), ha="right", family=fable.BODY_STACK,
                size=8, color=fable.FAINT, zorder=7,   # knocks out even the lobe stroke
                path_effects=[pe.withStroke(linewidth=3.4, foreground=fable.PAPER)])
for spoke_deg in range(-90, 91, 30):
    spoke = np.deg2rad(spoke_deg)
    ax.plot([0, np.sin(spoke)], [0, np.cos(spoke)],
            lw=0.7, color=fable.HAIRLINE, zorder=0)
    ax.annotate((f"{spoke_deg:+d}°" if spoke_deg else "0°").replace("-", "−"),
                (1.06 * np.sin(spoke), 1.06 * np.cos(spoke)),
                ha="center", va="center", family=fable.BODY_STACK, size=9,
                color=fable.MUTED)

# the pattern: context in grey, the main lobe in violet
main_lobe = np.abs(angle_deg) <= 14.4                    # first nulls of the 8-element array
ax.plot(pattern_x, pattern_y, lw=1.6, color=fable.CONTEXT)
ax.plot(pattern_x[main_lobe], pattern_y[main_lobe], lw=2.6, color=fable.ACCENT)
ax.fill(np.append(pattern_x[main_lobe], 0), np.append(pattern_y[main_lobe], 0),
        color=fable.ACCENT, alpha=0.08, lw=0)

# the −3 dB beamwidth, measured on the figure (label inside the empty lobe)
brace = np.deg2rad(np.linspace(half_power_angles[0], half_power_angles[-1], 60))
brace_r = db_to_radius(-3)
ax.plot(brace_r * np.sin(brace), brace_r * np.cos(brace), lw=1.4, color=fable.INK)
ax.annotate(f"{beamwidth:.1f}°\nat −3 dB", (0, brace_r), xytext=(0, -13),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="center", va="top",
            family=fable.BODY_STACK, weight=700, size=9.5, color=fable.INK,
            path_effects=[pe.withStroke(linewidth=2.6, foreground=fable.PAPER)])

# first sidelobe, labelled with its level
fable.mark(ax, pattern_x[sidelobe_index], pattern_y[sidelobe_index],
           f"first sidelobe\n{sidelobe_db:.1f} dB".replace("-", "−"),
           dx=26, dy=6, color=fable.MUTED)

ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(-1.18, 1.18)
ax.set_ylim(-0.06, 1.18)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

Notice what carried over from A1 even with the axes gone: the page anatomy, the ink roles
(hairline furniture, muted labels, one accent), printed values paying the debt of a
non-standard form, and the annotation budget spent on *the two numbers an RF engineer would
ask for first* — beamwidth and sidelobe level.

::: {.callout-important}
## Extract — the bespoke rules
1. **Draw the furniture first, quietly** — rings and spokes in `HAIRLINE`/`FAINT` so the
   data owns the contrast.
2. **Measure on the figure**: the beamwidth brace and sidelobe label are computed from the
   data in the cell, never transcribed constants.
3. Domain geometry beats chart convention *when the reader's question is geometric* —
   "where does the energy go" is an angle, so the figure is angular.
:::

# Capstone — the datasheet page

**Principle.** Everything at once: a `study`-register page that reads like the first page of
a component datasheet. Hero numbers answer the skim; four panels answer the read; spec bands
and marks answer the engineer. One header, one source line, one system.

```{python}
#| label: capstone-datasheet
#| fig-cap: "DUT-042, one page: stat row for the skim, measurement panels for the read, spec limits and P1dB marked for the engineer. The twin-axis temptation is answered with stacked shared-x panels."
dut = load("rf_dut_report")
frequency_ghz = dut["freq_ghz"]
power_amp = load("rf_pa_efficiency")
drive_dbm = power_amp["pin_dbm"]
pa_gain_db = power_amp["gain_db"]
pae_pct = power_amp["pae_pct"]

# measure first — the title must say what the data says (the gain does fail at the edge)
GAIN_SPEC_DB = 18.0
spec_cross_ghz = frequency_ghz[dut["gain_db"] < GAIN_SPEC_DB][0]

fable.theme("study")
fig, panels = fable.page(
    size=(10.2, 8.6),
    mosaic="abcd\nGGRR\nNNPP\nNNEE",
    kicker="DUT-042 · wideband LNA · rev B silicon",
    title=f"Meets spec to {spec_cross_ghz:.1f} GHz — gain clips the 18 dB floor at the band edge",
    dek="Measured at 25 °C, Vdd 3.3 V, 50 Ω. Shaded regions fail spec; the dashed rules are the limits.",
    source="Source: synthesized DUT report + PA sweep (data/build_datasets.py)",
    note="sheet 1 of 1 · fable",
    height_ratios=[0.8, 2, 2, 2], hspace=0.5, wspace=0.42,
)

gain_db_meas = dut["gain_db"]
noise_figure_db = dut["noise_figure_db"]
return_loss_db = dut["return_loss_db"]
small_signal_gain = pa_gain_db[:5].mean()
p1db_index = int(np.argmin(np.abs(pa_gain_db - (small_signal_gain - 1))))

fable.stat(panels["a"], f"{gain_db_meas.max():.1f} dB", "peak gain", "at 1.0 GHz")
fable.stat(panels["b"], f"{noise_figure_db.min():.2f} dB", "best noise figure", "at 1.5 GHz")
fable.stat(panels["c"], f"{drive_dbm[p1db_index]:.1f} dBm", "input P1dB", "PA sweep")
fable.stat(panels["d"], f"{pae_pct.max():.0f}%", "peak PAE", "at full drive")

gain_ax = panels["G"]
gain_ax.plot(frequency_ghz, gain_db_meas, color=fable.ACCENT)
gain_ax.set_ylim(15, 24)
fable.panel_title(gain_ax, "Gain vs frequency")
fable.finish(gain_ax)
fable.spec_band(gain_ax, GAIN_SPEC_DB, side="below", label="18 dB min")
fable.units(gain_ax, "y", "db")
fable.units(gain_ax, "x", "ghz")
fable.mark(gain_ax, spec_cross_ghz, GAIN_SPEC_DB,
           f"under spec beyond {spec_cross_ghz:.2f} GHz",
           dx=-88, dy=-26, color=fable.BAD, size=8)

return_ax = panels["R"]
return_ax.plot(frequency_ghz, return_loss_db, color=fable.NAVY)
return_ax.set_ylim(-25, -8)
fable.panel_title(return_ax, "Input return loss")
fable.finish(return_ax)
fable.spec_band(return_ax, -10, side="above", label="−10 dB max")
fable.units(return_ax, "y", "db")
fable.units(return_ax, "x", "ghz")

noise_ax = panels["N"]
noise_ax.plot(frequency_ghz, noise_figure_db, color=fable.EMERALD)
noise_ax.set_ylim(1.0, 2.2)
fable.panel_title(noise_ax, "Noise figure")
fable.finish(noise_ax)
fable.spec_band(noise_ax, 2.0, side="above", label="2.0 dB max")
fable.units(noise_ax, "y", "db")
fable.units(noise_ax, "x", "ghz")

# The dual-axis temptation, resolved: gain and PAE share the drive axis,
# not a scale — so they get stacked panels, x shared, one unit each.
compression_ax = panels["P"]
compression_ax.plot(drive_dbm, pa_gain_db, color=fable.ACCENT)
compression_ax.scatter([drive_dbm[p1db_index]], [pa_gain_db[p1db_index]],
                       s=30, color=fable.INK, zorder=5)
compression_ax.annotate("P1dB", (drive_dbm[p1db_index], pa_gain_db[p1db_index]),
                        xytext=(8, 4), textcoords="offset points",
                        family=fable.BODY_STACK, weight=700, size=8.5, color=fable.INK)
compression_ax.set_ylim(11, 16)
fable.panel_title(compression_ax, "PA gain compression")
fable.finish(compression_ax, nbins=4)
fable.units(compression_ax, "y", "db")
fable.units(compression_ax, "x", "dbm")   # its own scale — a borrowed axis doesn't read

efficiency_ax = panels["E"]
efficiency_ax.sharex(compression_ax)
efficiency_ax.plot(drive_dbm, pae_pct, color=fable.OCHRE)
# solid, labelled: dashed strokes are reserved for spec limits on this sheet
efficiency_ax.axvline(drive_dbm[p1db_index], lw=0.9, color=fable.FAINT, zorder=0)
efficiency_ax.annotate("P1dB", (drive_dbm[p1db_index], 57), xytext=(4, 0),
                       textcoords="offset points", family=fable.BODY_STACK,
                       size=8, color=fable.MUTED)
efficiency_ax.set_ylim(0, 60)
fable.panel_title(efficiency_ax, "Power-added efficiency")
fable.finish(efficiency_ax, nbins=4)
fable.units(efficiency_ax, "y", "pct")
fable.units(efficiency_ax, "x", "dbm")

fable.save(fig, "dut042_datasheet")
```

The compression/efficiency pair is the deliberate lesson: the M7 capstone twinned them on one
axes with colour-keyed spines — legal, but the reader still juggles two scales. Stacked
shared-x panels give each quantity its own honest axis, and the faint P1dB rule ties the story
together across both. When in doubt, **split, don't twin.**

::: {.callout-important}
## Extract — the capstone rules
1. **The page scales up**: kicker/title/dek/source work unchanged for a 9-panel mosaic —
   one header block, one source line, per-panel micro-titles.
2. **Stat tiles answer the skim** before any axes are read — put the numbers a skimmer
   needs in `fable.stat()` tiles, computed from the data.
3. **Split, don't twin**: stacked shared-x panels with one unit each beat a dual-y axes;
   a faint shared rule (P1dB) carries the correspondence.
:::

# The whole system, distilled {.unnumbered}

| Chapter | Principle | The lever it left behind |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | focused beats decluttered | `page(kicker, title, dek, source)` — the anatomy |
| **S2** | one dataset, three readers | `theme("glance" / "read" / "study")` — the register |
| **S3** | colour claims are computable | `check_palette.py` · `SERIES` · `SEQUENTIAL`/`DIVERGING` |
| **S4** | craft is a budget | the altitude ladder + the four-gate A2 test |
| **S5** | some data has its own geometry | furniture-first bespoke drawing, values printed |
| **S6** | the page scales to a datasheet | `stat()` tiles · `spec_band()` · split-don't-twin |

The three questions — *what am I saying, who is reading, how hard should I try* — plus the
guide's chart choice cover every figure decision this repo knows how to make. The rules live
in [`STYLE_AND_SUBSTANCE.md`](../STYLE_AND_SUBSTANCE.md); the lever is one import away:

```python
import fable
fable.theme("read")
```
